newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumer credit growth leveled off in June.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumer credit growth leveled off in June.

text.p: Consumers curbed their use of credit in June, paying off new-car loans instead of taking out more as total debts leveled off for the first time in more than four years, the Federal Reserve said Thursday.
U.S. consumer instalment credit was unchanged in June after rising a revised $2.5 billion at a 2.5 percent annual rate in May, the Fed said.
It was the first time since May 1993 -- when consumer credit shrank by $700 million -- that instalment credit failed to grow month-by-month.
Previously, the Fed said that May consumer credit had risen by $3 billion but it revised that estimate down.
In June, auto credit outstanding fell by $100 million at a 0.2 percent annual rate following a $100 million increase in May at a 0.4 percent rate.

Other credit, a catch-all category that includes consumer bank loans like those taken out for mobile homes and to pay for education but not home equity loans or mortgages, fell $2.4 billion at a 9.5 percent annual rate in June. In May, this category of credit rose $600 million at an 2.5 percent annual rate.

But there was a significant increase in revolving, or credit-card, credit, which grew by $2.5 billion at a 5.8 percent annual rate in June, the Fed said. Credit-card debt had risen $1.7 billion at a 4.1 percent rate in May.
The Fed said its revolving credit category has been expanded to include the revolving debt held by finance companies and the "other" category has been reduced by the same amount.
The current dollar value of all outstanding consumer credit in June was $1.211 trillion, up from $1.147 trillion a year earlier in June 1996.
